title: Franck Migone
text:
I work at the intersection of official statistics, public policy, and data science. Since 2021, I have worked at Côte d’Ivoire’s National Agency of Statistics (ANSTAT), where I serve as Deputy Director for Methodological Innovation and Head of DataLaB, ANSTAT’s data innovation lab.
My work explores how artificial intelligence, big data, and modern survey methods can improve economic measurement and public decision-making. I am particularly interested in labor markets, poverty, and economic development in Côte d’Ivoire and West Africa.

title: Franck Migone
text:
Current focus

Economic measurement: labor markets, poverty, education, and household welfare.
Statistical innovation: AI, satellite imagery, big data, and survey methods.
Knowledge sharing: teaching econometrics and sampling, and writing about economics and data.

title: Research

title: Research
section: Fiscalité, informalité, transferts et pauvreté en Côte d’Ivoire: une analyse d’incidence sur l’EHCVM 2021
text:
Fiscalité, informalité, transferts et pauvreté en Côte d’Ivoire: une analyse d’incidence sur l’EHCVM 2021
With Armand Djaha and N’Dre Lebe
Working paper · Read the paper · Replication code

Résumé. Cette étude mesure l’incidence des impôts et des dépenses publiques en Côte d’Ivoire à partir de l’EHCVM 2021, dans une analyse Commitment to Equity ancrée sur la consommation par personne. Elle combine barèmes fiscaux, budgets exécutés et tableau national des ressources et des emplois, en tenant compte des achats informels. Sous l’hypothèse conditionnelle S3, le Gini passe de 0,3409 pour le revenu primaire à 0,3167 pour le revenu final. La pauvreté monétaire atteint toutefois 42,04 % au revenu consommable, contre 37,72 % au revenu primaire, et 4,35 % de la population devient nouvellement pauvre. Après valorisation de l’éducation et de la santé publiques, le taux associé au revenu final tombe à 33,92 %, mais ce coût public n’est pas une ressource monétaire. Dans une simulation comptable à quantités fixes, une TVA de 9 % sur certaines ventes finales accroît la pauvreté de 0,47 point sans compensation; le recyclage intégral de la recette par personne la réduit de 0,22 point.

title: Research
section: Job Quality and Poverty in Developing Countries: Evidence from Côte d’Ivoire
text:
Job Quality and Poverty in Developing Countries: Evidence from Côte d’Ivoire
Working paper · Read the paper

Abstract. This study analyzes the influence of household members’ job quality on household poverty status in Côte d’Ivoire using data from the 2018 Harmonized Survey of Household Living Conditions. Using simple probit regressions, the study highlights the significant negative effect of a household head’s job quality on household poverty risk. It also shows that improving the job quality of other household members reduces the risk of household poverty. In addition to promoting improved employment conditions for workers, policymakers should promote women’s access to high-quality jobs. This could involve investing in social facilities to relieve the burden of caring for children in the household.

title: Research
section: The Causal Impact of Armed Conflict on Education Outcomes in Mali
text:
The Causal Impact of Armed Conflict on Education Outcomes in Mali
With Josias Sadia
Working paper · Read the paper

Abstract. This study, using a double-difference methodology and propensity score matching, analyses the causal impact of Mali’s prolonged crises and conflicts on the Malian education system. The results indicate that these events have had a significant and negative impact on education, resulting in a drop in the average number of years of education between the generations that attended school during the conflict and the previous generation, ranging from 1.13 to 1.97 years of education. These findings underline the urgency of taking measures to mitigate these adverse effects and re-establish a functional education system in the country, highlighting the importance of understanding the causal impact of the crises on education in Mali.

title: Research
section: Exposure to Violence and Academic Performance Among Adolescents in Côte d’Ivoire
text:
Exposure to Violence and Academic Performance Among Adolescents in Côte d’Ivoire
With Sekongo Coulibaly
Working paper · Read the paper

Abstract. This study analyzes the effects of exposure to violence on the academic performance of children aged 13 to 18 in Côte d’Ivoire. We examine how physical, emotional, and sexual abuse affect students’ academic performance using data from the 2018 Violence Against Children Survey. The results show that 76.66% of the children in our sample report having experienced at least one form of violence and display more pronounced academic difficulties than those not exposed. A binary probit regression indicates that physical and emotional violence significantly increase the likelihood of school dropout and grade delay, especially when perpetrated by close adults. Sexual violence does not show direct effects on academic outcomes in our sample, although it may lead to indirect consequences.

title: Research
section: Estimating Poverty with Satellite Imagery in Developing Countries: Evidence from Côte d’Ivoire
text:
Estimating Poverty with Satellite Imagery in Developing Countries: Evidence from Côte d’Ivoire
With Koné Kinin Mamadou, Kouamé Moussa Richard, Koné Djoudori Joachim, Kouassi Kouamé Aristide, and Doukouré Daouda
Working paper · Read the paper

Abstract. This study develops a methodology for estimating poverty in Côte d’Ivoire using Sentinel-2 satellite imagery and deep-learning transfer techniques. The approach follows a three-stage pipeline: pre-training a VGG16 convolutional neural network on ImageNet, fine-tuning it to predict nighttime light intensity from daytime imagery, and extracting visual features for poverty prediction. Using data from the 2018–2019 Harmonized Household Living Conditions Survey covering 12,992 households, visual features are enriched with spectral indices including NO₂ concentration, land surface temperature, and the Enhanced Normalized Difference Impervious Surface Index. The best model achieves an R² of 40.15%, with predictions remarkably consistent with survey data: 39.98% predicted versus 39.44% observed in 2018, and 37.86% versus 37.50% in 2021. Temporal validation confirms the approach’s capacity to capture poverty dynamics, offering a cost-effective complementary tool for monitoring poverty between survey waves in Sub-Saharan Africa.
